papers.title: The Price of Hard Coverage Constraints in Online Conformal Prediction
papers.abstract: Conformal prediction provides distribution-free uncertainty quantification, but in sequential deployment, standard coverage guarantees can still allow substantial fluctuations in the number of miscoverages over time. We study an online setting in which prediction sets are produced one round at a time and the cumulative number of miscoverages must stay within a prescribed budget throughout deployment.Such a hard coverage guarantee can be enforced by enlarging prediction sets, but how much additional prediction-set size is fundamentally necessary remains unclear. We characterize this unavoidable efficiency cost over $T$ prediction rounds. Remarkably, the cost persists even with i.i.d.\ data, a known score distribution, and perfect knowledge of the population-optimal prediction set. Under suitable regularity conditions relating coverage and prediction-set size, we determine the minimum cumulative excess prediction-set size required by any online method satisfying the hard coverage constraint. This minimum cost is $\Theta(\log T)$ for expected cost at a fixed time known in advance, $\Theta(T^{1/3})$ for the largest expected cost over all fixed times up to $T$, and $\Theta(\sqrt{T})$ for the expected worst realized cost when the evaluation time is chosen in hindsight. We further show that these rates can be attained using past scores, without knowing the score distribution. Thus, even perfect statistical knowledge does not make sequential reliability free.

papers.title: Optimal Min-Entropy Estimation with High Probability
papers.abstract: Min-entropy plays a fundamental role in assessing the unpredictability of randomness sources. In particular, NIST SP 800-90B specifies min-entropy estimation as a key procedure for entropy sources used in cryptographic random bit generators, illustrating the practical importance of reliable min-entropy estimation. In this paper, we settle the sample complexity of min-entropy estimation with high probability in both the classical and quantum cases. Specifically, for min-entropy estimation with additive error $\varepsilon$ and probability at least $1-\delta$, the sample complexity is $\Theta(d\log(d/\delta)/\varepsilon^2)$ for classical distributions on $d$ symbols and $\Theta((d^2+d\log(1/\delta))/\varepsilon^2)$ for quantum states on a $d$-dimensional Hilbert space. Our results admit short and simple proofs.

papers.title: Multiply Robust Causal Mediation Analysis with Continuous Treatments
papers.abstract: In many applications, researchers are interested in the direct and indirect causal effects of a treatment or exposure on an outcome of interest. Mediation analysis offers a rigorous framework for identifying and estimating these causal effects. For binary treatments, efficient estimators for the direct and indirect effects are presented by Tchetgen Tchetgen and Shpitser (2012) based on the influence function of the parameter of interest. These estimators possess desirable properties such as multiple-robustness and asymptotic normality while allowing for slower than root-n rates of convergence for the nuisance parameters. However, in settings involving continuous treatments, these influence function-based estimators are not readily applicable without making strong parametric assumptions. In this work, utilizing a kernel smoothing approach, we propose an estimator suitable for settings with continuous treatments inspired by the influence function-based estimation strategy. Our proposed approach employs cross-fitting, relaxing the smoothness requirements on the nuisance functions and allowing them to be estimated at slower rates than the target parameter. Additionally, similar to influence function-based estimators, our proposed estimator is multiply robust and asymptotically normal, allowing for inference in settings where parametric assumptions may not be justified.

papers.title: On Minimal Observation Time for Recovering Latent Hawkes Networks
papers.abstract: Dynamics of interacting systems in engineering, society, and nature often evolve over latent networks that govern which entities can interact. We study the problem of inferring these networks from event-based observations, which arise naturally in finance, seismology, and neuroscience. While there is substantial algorithmic work addressing this important problem, theoretical results are scarce. In this paper we ask the following fundamental question: what is the minimum time that one must observe the dynamics in order to exactly recover the underlying network, as a function of the number $d$ of interacting entities? For a class of stationary Hawkes processes with sparse, weak interactions, we prove that an observation time of order $\log d$ is sufficient and necessary. For the upper bound we construct a two-stage estimator that uses clipped and binned event data for screening, followed by a least-squares refinement, and apply concentration bounds derived from the Poisson cluster representation. For the lower bound we combine Fano's inequality with Jacod's Girsanov formula for point processes on a suitable subclass of networks.

papers.title: Bidirectional Random Projections
papers.abstract: This paper analyzes bidirectional random projections for ordinary least squares (OLS) regression under the fixed design setting. Let $(X, Y) \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times p}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}$ be a sample and $W \in \mathbb{R}^{n_1\times n}$, $R \in \mathbb{R}^{p\times p_1}$ be two random projections. We develop an expected excess loss bound for the OLS estimator built on $(WXR, WY)$, extending an established bound for the OLS estimator built on $(XR, Y)$. Our analysis shows that our bound is larger and the gap between the two bounds decays at a rate of approximately $O(1/n_1)$. These findings are confirmed by numerical results.

papers.title: Not All Mislabels Are Equal: Efficient Task-Aware Auditing with Confidence Sequences
papers.abstract: We study efficient, adaptive auditing of categorical labels in a fixed dataset, motivated by biodiversity credit programs in which expert verification of species records is costly and downstream scores (e.g., payment) are more sensitive to errors on certain labels than on others. Our proposed ATLAS framework couples anytime-valid inference with a task-aware adaptive auditing policy. Representing label corrections through a confusion matrix, we prioritize which data points to inspect next based on both label uncertainty and the influence of potential label corrections on the downstream score function. In our main case study on Kenyan biodiversity data, task-aware auditing reduces the expert review needed to estimate both the mislabel rate and the nonlinear biodiversity score while maintaining anytime-valid guarantees. We also evaluate ATLAS on public datasets for image classification and named-entity recognition. Across our experiments with linear and nonlinear scores, ATLAS generally reaches the same precision as competing anytime-valid methods with substantially fewer audits. When distribution-free guarantees are prohibitively costly, we develop a model-based Bayesian alternative that can further reduce the number of audits by relying on modeling assumptions. Our biodiversity case study highlights a gap between statistical validity and practical feasibility: generic methods such as Serfling's bound and existing confidence-sequence procedures are rigorous but can require prohibitively many expert reviews in practice. Together, these results show task-aware auditing can significantly reduce the number of expert audits needed while providing finite-sample, anytime-valid guarantees

papers.title: Long-Term Quantile Treatment Effects with Combined Experimental and Observational Data
papers.abstract: This paper studies the identification, estimation, and inference of long-term quantile treatment effects (LTQTEs) when short-term experimental data are supplemented with long-term observational data. Under a latent unconfoundedness framework, we establish identification of the LTQTE curve and derive the corresponding efficient influence functions. Building on these influence functions, we propose a semiparametrically efficient estimation procedure and develop a multiplier bootstrap method for uniform inference on the LTQTE curve, yielding valid simultaneous confidence bands over a continuum of quantile indices.

papers.title: Exact and Approximate Maximum Likelihood Estimation for Multivariate Diffusions under High-Frequency Sampling
papers.abstract: We establish the asymptotic theory of the exact maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) for discretely observed multivariate ergodic diffusions under high-frequency, long-span sampling, solving an open problem posed by \citet{YCW2019} and \citet{Li2013}. The drift may grow linearly, and the volatility is bounded away from zero and either bounded or proportional to $1+|x|$. When the sampling interval decays polynomially, the exact MLE is consistent, asymptotically normal and efficient, with rates $\sqrt{n\Delta_n}$ for drift and $\sqrt n$ for diffusion parameters. Under an additional condition on ergodic averages, and when the time span $n\Delta_n$ also grows polynomially, its moments converge as well. The proof never analyzes the exact likelihood directly: it shows that a closed-form density expansion of sufficiently high order is uniformly accurate in relative terms at every observed transition, so that the two log-likelihoods differ by $o_P(1)$ uniformly in the parameter. The same argument yields accuracy conditions under which an approximate likelihood is asymptotically equivalent to the exact one; in particular, the approximate MLE of Yang, Chen and Wan converges to the true parameter. For the delta-expansion estimator of fixed order $K\ge1$, we derive the leading bias explicitly. It shows that $n\Delta_n^{K+1}\to0$ cannot be weakened when the bias constant is nonzero, and that the bias falls on the drift parameters for even $K$ and on the diffusion parameters for odd $K$. Monte Carlo experiments confirm the predicted biases.

papers.title: When Is Membership Graded? Identifiability and Resolution Limits of a Graded Gaussian Mixture Model
papers.abstract: Mixed-membership models describe each unit as a graded blend of latent types. Before the blend is interpreted, the data should be able to rule out the simpler story in which every unit belongs to a single type. We ask when they can, in a scalar graded Gaussian mixture model, in which each observation is a Beta-weighted convex combination of independent Gaussian draws from two types, the mechanism behind functional mixed-membership models and the normal compositional model. The model is identifiable, unequal variances included, but the identifying information sits in the far tails of the marginal. For the symmetric model we give a closed-form hard-membership mixture that matches the graded marginal in five cumulants, and a Le Cam bound turns it into a certified sample size below which no test separates graded from hard membership with summed error under one half. The threshold is governed by the concentration $c$ relative to $c_0\approx d^2$, where $d$ is the type half-separation in within-type standard deviations. At $d=3$ it is about 2,600 observations at $c=3$ and 77,000 at $c=6$. Most of the difficulty comes from learning $c$. On 100 simulated datasets with graded membership, a correctly specified posterior under the default priors of a published Bayesian sampler for this model class reports hard membership every time, a weak prior gives intervals for the concentration spanning orders of magnitude, and the sampler's own answers depend on where it starts.

papers.title: Simultaneous analysis of approximate leave-one-out cross-validation and mean-field inference II: General convex penalties
papers.abstract: For smooth penalties and group Lasso, analyzed approximate leave-one-out (ALO) cross-validation by comparing its weights with the trace correction used in mean-field inference. For a $C^2$ penalty $R$, the matrix entering these corrections is $A=[\nabla^2R(\widehat b)+X^TDX]^{-1}$, where $\widehat b$ is the full-data estimator and $D$ is the diagonal matrix of fitted loss curvatures; for group Lasso, the penalty and loss curvatures are first restricted to the active support before taking the pseudoinverse. The obstacle to extending this argument to general convex penalties was the lack of an explicit formula for the matrix $A$ entering these corrections. For every finite-valued strongly convex penalty, we construct such a matrix from ordinary derivatives of the penalty response at the observed subgradient. Its projection--pseudoinverse formula separates the response space and penalty curvature, fixed by conditioning, from the explicit design dependence. This supplies the missing ingredient to extend the probabilistic argument of Part~I. The construction recovers the inverse Hessian for smooth penalties and the active-group inverse for group Lasso, including inactive boundary groups. In the proportional regime, for Gaussian designs with general positive-definite covariance and covariance-scaled strong convexity, we obtain unconditional bounds comparing both ALO and mean-field predictions with exact leave-one-out predictions in regression and single-index models. The expected average squared prediction error is $O(n^{-1})$, and the expected absolute criterion error is $O(n^{-1/2})$, under bounded, 1-Lipschitz loss scores and suitable test functions. The matrix and ALO weights use only observed data; the mean-field correction additionally uses the design covariance. The construction, recovery identities and statistical guarantees are formalized in Lean~4.

papers.title: Training Neural Networks to be Locally Adaptive
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks fitted by global empirical risk minimization commit to a single model for the entire covariate space. In a regression problem, if the regression function $f_0$ is inhomogeneous --- varying rapidly in one region, while being nearly flat in another --- no single model can be appropriate everywhere, and the fit degrades where the function varies most rapidly. Here we study an alternative in which, instead of fitting the network globally, we fit it locally. For each query point $x$, a \emph{local neural network} is trained on the $k$ nearest-neighbours of $x$ alone, making the training sample and the fitted function query-dependent. We analyze the performance of the resulting estimator through a localization approach, establishing that the pointwise risk of the estimator with an appropriate choice of $k$ attains the rate $n^{-2\alpha/(2\alpha+d^{*})}$, up to logarithmic factors, when $f_0$ is locally $\alpha$-H\"older with $\alpha\in(0,1]$ and the covariates are supported on a $d^{*}$-dimensional manifold embedded in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$. A matching Le Cam lower bound shows that this rate is pointwise minimax optimal. However, the local rate-optimality requires $k$ to be calibrated to the smoothness of $f_0$, which is unknown in practice. We therefore provide a locally adaptive choice of $k$ that makes the neural network adapt to the local H\"older exponent of $f_0$ and to the intrinsic dimension simultaneously, both of which are potentially varying over the covariate domain. An extensive simulation study demonstrates the dominance of the locally adaptive neural network over a globally trained network and several state-of-the-art methods.

papers.title: Anytime-valid inference for conditional hazard and survival functions with streaming data
papers.abstract: We consider the nonparametric estimation of the conditional hazard, cumulative hazard and survival functions of a time-to-event variable from streaming data subject to censoring, truncation, or a cure fraction. A time-to-event model is a map from the distribution of the latent variables to that of the observed ones. For a large class of models this map has an explicit inverse, and the conditional hazard is the ratio of the density of the exactly observed durations to an at-risk function. Both are estimated by one-pass learners, in which each observation contributes once and is never revised, such as recursive kernel, series and histogram estimators. Our main result is an asymptotic confidence band sequence for the conditional hazard at a fixed covariate value, uniform in time and in the sample size, which allows monitoring after a burn-in, and stopping at a data-dependent time. The band can shrink at the optimal uniform rate up to a logarithmic factor. Bands for the cumulative hazard and the survival function follow. In simulations, a fixed-sample band inspected repeatedly fails in about half of the streams, while the miscoverage of the recommended bands stays below, or close to, the nominal level.

papers.title: Bivariate Renyi Tsallis Divergence
papers.abstract: In this paper, a bivariate extension of the differential Renyi Tsallis divergence is introduced for comparing two absolutely continuous bivariate probability distributions. Fundamental properties of the proposed divergence are studied, including non negativity, pseudo additivity under component wise independence, and invariance under monotone and nonsingular linear transformations. Relationships with Renyi, Tsallis, alpha, Bhattacharyya, and Hellinger divergence measures are also established. A sensitivity analysis is performed to compare the Renyi, Tsallis and Renyi Tsallis divergences under the Marshall Olkin and Gumbel type bivariate exponential models, taking the magnitude of Kendall's rank correlation coefficient as a common scale for dependence. The proposed measure is further developed for bivariate order statistics, with particular emphasis on the joint distribution of the minimum and maximum order statistics for several lifetime distributions, including exponential, Weibull, Pareto, and Rayleigh models. When the underlying distributions are unknown, a nonparametric estimator is constructed using bivariate Gaussian kernel density estimators with plug in bandwidth selection. The proposed estimator is applied to a real life dataset and bootstrap resampling is used to assess estimation uncertainty. The results show the applicability of the proposed divergence for comparing bivariate distributions and indicate that its finite sample performance depends on the order parameter and the distributions being compared.

papers.title: Covariate-Indexed Inclusion Probabilities on Unbalanced Panels
papers.abstract: We estimate the probability that an item with given covariates belongs to a set when the cross-section changes over time and items and periods are dependent. We propose two convex models whose fitted probabilities are nonnegative by construction and remain valid whatever the dependence between items, for which we establish consistency, finite-sample bounds and limit distributions for serially dependent panels. One suits events of moderate or high probability, the other rare events, and half the disagreement between their fits estimates a lower bound on the misspecification error of the worse fit, without knowledge of the true probabilities. On monthly US stock failures, the rare-event model predicts better than the ordinary logit and the classical failure logit. With the eight classical predictors, most of the gain comes from basis functions of the rank angle of each predictor and summary.

papers.title: Testing the Pareto law through a Stein-Laplace characterization
papers.abstract: A Stein--Laplace characterization yields two closed-form goodness-of-fit statistics for the Pareto type-I family with unknown shape and known lower endpoint. The signed integral statistic $T_n$ has a standard normal limit after studentization, but explicit non-Pareto alternatives show that it is not omnibus consistent. The integrated squared discrepancy $S_n$ yields a consistent test against every fixed non-Pareto alternative on the specified support with a finite, positive logarithmic moment. We derive the weighted chi-square null limit of $nS_n$ and give conditions for an asymptotically valid parametric-bootstrap and plug-in covariance-operator method. The latter uses Nystr\"om eigenvalue approximation to avoid repeated sample generation and parameter estimation. A large Monte Carlo comparison study shows competitive performance relative to existing procedures in the literature. In the paired study, the two calibrations have similar empirical power, with slightly higher small-sample rejection rates for the bootstrap in some settings. In the timing experiment, covariance-operator calibration is approximately $28$--$37$ times faster at $n=200$. An exploratory threshold-sensitivity analysis of Danish fire-insurance losses illustrates the dependence of Pareto goodness-of-fit conclusions on the specified tail region.

papers.title: Identifiability of latent variable models with flexible latent distributions
papers.abstract: Latent variable models are popularly used to characterize dependence among many observed variables through underlying latent variables. Recent advances in statistics and machine learning methods have encouraged growing interest in studying latent variable models with flexible latent distributions that capture complex latent structures. This flexibility, however, raises a fundamental question of whether model parameters can be identified when the latent distribution is unknown and must itself be learned. In this paper, we show that exact identifiability fails almost everywhere, in the sense that distinct but arbitrarily close pairs of model parameters and latent distributions can yield exactly the same distribution for the observed variables. Nonetheless, the resulting identification ambiguity is small. In particular, we prove that the identification ambiguity, measured by the diameter of the set of parameters inducing the same marginal distribution, vanishes at a superpolynomial rate of $\exp\{-c(\log p)^2\}$ as the number of observed variables $p$ grows. Building on this result, we show that the failure of exact identifiability need not preclude consistent estimation or valid inference of the model parameters and latent distribution. These results suggest that, when many variables are observed, the identifiability issue is far less of an obstacle to estimation and inference in latent variable models than is commonly expected.

papers.title: Asymptotics of Gibbs Posterior Measures on Infinite-Dimensional Hypothesis Spaces
papers.abstract: We prove almost sure contraction rates and consistency for Gibbs posterior measures on arbitrary hypothesis spaces, in general infinite dimensional, under dependent data, nonadditive and time-dependent losses and learning rates, misspecified models, and unattainable minimisers of the limiting objective. In particular, we develop a novel proof approach in contraction rate theory by studying the asymptotics of Gibbs measures through Lorentz spaces, real interpolation theory, and Laplace transforms dispensing with testing or variational formulations which are unavailable in the considered generality. As a consequence we obtain almost sure contraction rates for dominated Bayes and fractional Bayes posterior measures in the same generality, extending existing theory on misspecified Bayesian inference. Furthermore, we demonstrate our theoretical results on novel applications to Gibbs posteriors for Dirichlet process priors with a nonadditive Wasserstein metric loss function under ergodic, non-Markovian observables.

papers.title: A mechanistic characterization of missingness at random
papers.abstract: The missingness-at-random (MAR) assumption underlying many missing-data methods describes abstract statistical independences, whereas practitioners reason more naturally about the causal mechanisms that generate missingness. To bridge this gap, we provide a mechanistic characterization of MAR in terms of paths in a directed acyclic graph (DAG) modified to allow certain edges to cease to operate when an incomplete variable is missing, a property termed "context-specific causal irrelevance (CSCI)". Under a faithfulness condition, MAR holds if and only if the modified DAG contains no MAR-violating paths. Without CSCI, this condition reduces to a previously established d-separation condition, VMAR; thus, MAR without VMAR requires specific kinds of CSCI, as can occur with monotone dropout. These results shift the burden on investigators from passively invoking MAR to justifying, on substantive grounds, the specific mechanisms it requires. We then consider identification of a target law p(v) of variables V by a MAR-assuming analysis, e.g., multiple imputation, that includes complete auxiliary variables Z (variables not in V). Barring a perfect cancellation, such an analysis recovers p(v) if and only if MAR holds with respect to V and Z jointly. We show that if there exists any set of auxiliaries such that (V, Z) obeys MAR, then the complete candidate auxiliaries that are ancestors of the target variables or their missingness indicators form a sufficient set. Contrary to standard recommendations, not all candidate auxiliaries should be used: even complete auxiliaries can introduce MAR violations that would not otherwise occur. We illustrate these results with simulations and an analysis of sexual identity change in the Stockholm Public Health Cohort, where our results indicate that a candidate auxiliary, income, should be excluded; including it attenuated estimates toward the null.

papers.title: COSI: A Framework for Robustly Valid Inference
papers.abstract: We introduce COSI (COnfidence from Scale Invariance), a framework for constructing confidence sets for statistical functionals. COSI builds on the HulC (Hull-based Confidence), which uses median unbiasedness to construct confidence sets from batch estimates. COSI uses scale-invariance properties shared by many common estimators. We divide the data into batches, compute an estimate in each batch, and retain each candidate parameter value for which the batch estimates pass a test of scale invariance. The resulting confidence sets are asymptotically valid under weaker assumptions than classical Wald and bootstrap procedures require, and their coverage can be closer to the nominal level in small samples. Applications include robust inference for the mean, regression coefficients in misspecified linear models, tensor norms, and Fr\'echet means.

papers.title: Greedy Empirical Bayes for Density Estimation
papers.abstract: Bayesian nonparametric density estimation is challenging in high dimensions, where traditional approaches like the Dirichlet process (DP) mixture rely on computationally intensive Markov chain Monte Carlo or approximations. We introduce the partition posterior bootstrap (PPB), where a flexible prior is constructed by smoothing a DP over a partition of the sample space. Conditioned on this partition, exact posterior sampling reduces to a simple Bayesian bootstrap-like algorithm. Importantly, we select the partition using a greedy empirical Bayes (GEB) algorithm which scales to high dimensions and large sample sizes. GEB greedily maximizes the closed-form marginal likelihood via local split decisions arising naturally from its factorization, yielding an adaptive binary tree partition. Our key theoretical result is that the GEB tree belongs to an admissible family with high probability, splitting all identifiable signals while avoiding over-splitting noise. As a result, the PPB posterior with the GEB tree attains adaptive contraction rates. Our theory holds under weak, verifiable assumptions, which we demonstrate in numerous examples. Empirically, PPB delivers accurate density estimates and uncertainty quantification at a fraction of the computational cost of other approaches, making it a practical off-the-shelf choice for high-dimensional Bayesian density estimation with theoretical guarantees.

papers.title: Refined Inference for Asymptotically Linear Estimators with Non-Negligible Second-Order Remainders
papers.abstract: First-order semiparametric inference typically uses the same influence-function linearization to justify both centering and sandwich variance estimation. We show that these are distinct questions. In a near-boundary regime, the second-order remainder can be nearly mean zero yet large enough to contribute O(n-1) sampling variation. When plug-in influence-function error and the cross term are negligible, the usual sandwich estimator captures only the influence-function component, and Wald intervals can undercover even when the point estimator is nearly unbiased. We derive a finite-sample variance decomposition and show that, when the cross term is asymptotically negligible, sandwich consistency is characterized by the condition nVar(Rrem) --> 0: the sandwich consistently estimates total variance in the strong-decay regime where this holds, and materially underestimates it in the near-boundary regime where nVar(Rrem) -->cR > 0. We then study two corrections. Under a leave-one-out remainder linearization condition, the jackknife consistently estimates the total variance; under a conditional Mallows-2 bootstrap condition, the pairs bootstrap does likewise. For clustered data we distinguish within-cluster dependence from first-order influence-function mismatch. Simulations for a surrogate-assisted targeted learning estimator in stepped-wedge cluster-randomized trials illustrate variance discrepancies and the limits of jackknife correction.

papers.title: Reconstructing the Probability Measure of a Multi-group Curie-Weiss Model with Interacting Groups
papers.abstract: We study the problem of reconstructing the probability measure of a multi-group version of the Curie-Weiss or mean-field model of ferromagnetism from a sample of the voting behaviour of the population. While originally used to study phase transitions in statistical mechanics, the Curie-Weiss model has been applied to study phenomena where many agents interact with each other, in particular in case of a heterogeneous population with identifiable subpopulations. The degree of social cohesion within social groups manifests in the way the members of the group influence each others' decisions as well as how they behave under outside influence from voters belonging to another group. While the maximum likelihood estimator of the coupling parameters has desirable statistical properties in theory, computational challenges make applications to larger populations impractical. Therefore, we analyse an estimator based on asymptotic approximations to the behaviour of the Curie-Weiss model valid for large populations. Due to the wide application of models such as Curie-Weiss, the estimator is potentially useful in disciplines such as political science, sociology, automated voting, and preference aggregation.

papers.title: A kernel method for the learning of Wasserstein geometric flows
papers.abstract: Wasserstein gradient and Hamiltonian flows provide geometric formulations of many partial differential equations. We develop a structure-preserving kernel method for jointly estimating the external potential and interaction kernel governing these flows, assuming a known internal energy. The inverse problem is formulated through a trajectory-dependent observation operator and regularized in a product of reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces, yielding an explicit finite representation of the estimator. We characterize joint non-identifiability through the null space of the observation operator and derive a Fourier criterion on the torus, distinguishing uniqueness of the regularized estimator from recovery of the underlying physical components. We establish reconstruction error bounds and convergence rates under source conditions and suitable regularization and mesh refinement, together with a stability estimate for Hamiltonian flows with vanishing internal energy. Numerical experiments demonstrate joint reconstruction and illustrate how unobservable interaction modes can prevent accurate potential recovery despite small observation-equation residuals. A comparison with sparse learning illustrates the dependence of reconstruction accuracy on the chosen dictionary.

papers.title: Asymptotics for Model Selection in Probabilistic Principal Component Analysis
papers.abstract: The probabilistic formulation of principal component analysis promises statistically grounded solutions to the problem of selecting the number of principal components. However, developing tractable model selection methods is complicated by the fact that the probabilistic principal component analysis (PPCA) model exhibits non-standard large sample asymptotics at model singularities, where the Fisher information matrix does not have full rank. In this work, tools from singular learning theory are used to provide a complete description of the marginal likelihood asymptotics for PPCA. The singular Bayesian information criterion (sBIC) along with our asymptotic results provides an effective procedure for selecting the number of principal components. In particular, the sBIC corrects for the overpenalization of the standard dimension-based BIC, which leads to too few principal components being selected, while also selecting the smallest true model with probability converging to one. Our framework extends beyond PPCA, where we also provide expressions for the sBIC that can be used to select between PPCA and factor analysis models. In both simulations and on real data the effectiveness of the proposed sBIC methodology is demonstrated.

papers.title: Spectral Recovery of Point Clouds from Noisy Geometric Graphs
papers.abstract: We study the problem of recovering low-dimensional latent geometry from a random geometric graph generated by noisy, high-dimensional data. Specifically, we analyze the performance of a spectral embedding algorithm on the Signal+Noise Graph Model, in which vertices are associated to points perturbed by Gaussian noise, and edges are included for pairs whose inner product exceeds a specified alignment threshold. In the high-dimensional regime where the number $n$ of points and the ambient dimension $d$ both tend to infinity, we show that under a spectral gap condition, the top eigenvectors and eigenvalues of the graph's adjacency matrix can be used to approximately recover the point cloud up to an orthogonal transformation. We illustrate our results on point clouds sampled from nested spheres and high-dimensional sinusoid curves.

papers.title: Canonical Layer Inference for Deep Gaussian Processes via Symmetry-Breaking Augmentation
papers.abstract: Deep Gaussian processes (DGPs) are flexible priors for estimating compositional functions, but function-level accuracy does not determine their intermediate-layer representations. The basic obstruction is an adjacent-layer symmetry: applying an invertible transformation and its inverse to two adjacent layers leaves the composed regression map unchanged. Under explicit symmetry and prior-comparability conditions, we show that the posterior may not concentrate on any prescribed intermediate-layer representation, even when the composed regression function is estimable. We introduce a layerwise exponential tilt of the DGP prior, using a penalty proportional to each hidden layer's distance from the identity map, with stronger weights on earlier layers. The methodology links an exact posterior-odds rule along likelihood-preserving symmetries to quantitative control of redundant layers. Under proxy and local prior-mass conditions, we derive a penalty window that preserves function-level fractional posterior contraction while localizing redundant layers at certain radius. The resulting design rule calibrates representation regularization to the function-estimation rate. It favors decompositions with earlier layers close to identity; uniqueness and automatic depth selection are not established. The general theory and methodology are supported with detailed examples.

papers.title: Sharp moderate deviations and uniform Berry--Esseen bounds for Hotelling's $T^2$-statistic via Stein's method
papers.abstract: Let $T^2_{H,n}$ denote the one-sample Hotelling statistic based on $n$ independent random vectors in $\mathbb R^d$ with a common mean, where $d\ge2$ is a fixed integer. Assume that the average covariance matrix is positive definite. We define the statistic to be zero when the centered sample covariance matrix is singular. Under the null hypothesis, we establish finite-sample Cram\'er-type moderate deviation results and uniform Berry--Esseen bounds under finite $p$th moments for $2<p\le3$. Explicit constructions show that the moderate deviation error order is optimal over independent triangular arrays. For identically distributed observations with a fixed distribution, we obtain \[ \sup_{0\le x\le b_n} \left| \frac{\mathbb P(T^2_{H,n}\ge x^2)} {\mathbb P(\chi_d^2\ge x^2)}-1 \right| = O\!\left((1+b_n)^p n^{-(p-2)/2}\right) \] for every nonnegative sequence $b_n=o(n^{(p-2)/(2p)})$. In this identically distributed setting, the uniform Berry--Esseen bound is $O(n^{-(p-2)/2})$. The proof uses a radial Stein identity and a recursive error estimate.

papers.title: Fundamental Limits of Honest Inference with Heterogeneous Transfer Sources
papers.abstract: Transfer learning can improve precision by borrowing information from external sources, but how much improvement is possible while maintaining valid inference? We address this by studying honest confidence intervals for a target parameter using multiple sources with heterogeneous prespecified discrepancy bounds. Under local information and admissibility conditions, we establish a universal lower bound on interval length for procedures maintaining uniform coverage. A scalar information equation characterizes the bound, revealing how precision depends jointly on source sample sizes and discrepancies. Large source samples need not yield greater precision gains when their discrepancies are large. When discrepancies are unrestricted, honest intervals cannot improve upon the target-only rate, even when all sources are unbiased. For the Gaussian location model, we calculate optimal source weights and construct honest intervals attaining the lower bound order, establishing sharpness. We extend the lower bound theory to semiparametric models through parametric submodels. For the Cox proportional hazards model, we verify the information conditions under which the lower bound applies, including under right censoring.

papers.title: Structural latent dimension: deterministic geometry and local Fisher structure
papers.abstract: We study the structural dimension of a second-order object: the minimum latent dimension that remains necessary relative to a declared class of competing dependence. Building on minimum-rank factor analysis and low-rank-plus-sparse decomposition, we use distances to lower-dimensional classes to describe inference near structural ambiguity. General distance and tangent-cone facts yield confidence statements and local margins. For rank-zero competitors with bounded residual degree, we derive exact maximum-weight $b$-matching formulas, support-slack tangent cones and sparse-spike angles; a shared residual support across a field can produce separation absent pointwise. We give positive-semidefinite brackets, a dimension-free Gaussian likelihood expansion, an exact quotient by the tangent of a low-rank background, and a detection floor from the margin. Equal-angle configurations with different branch multiplicities motivate static and spectral detection conjectures. Joint low-rank/residual profiling and the sharp composite information boundaries remain open.
